Two credit-card interest rates: chart where the payment goes before comparing the cost

Hold the monthly payment fixed while comparing two hypothetical ways of allocating the amount above a shared illustrative minimum across two balance buckets.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 5 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Compare allocation of payments across two interest-rate buckets

Interactive planning lab

Illustrative first minimum payment$213.75
Highest-first: completed payoff months30
Interest saving versus proportional excess allocation$239.64

Two invented interest-rate buckets with no new purchases, fees, grace periods or rate changes. Interest is opening monthly balance × nominal annual rate ÷ 12 before payment. The illustrative minimum is the lower of the statement total and the higher of CAD 25 or the entered statement percentage. Its allocation is proportional in both paths. Only excess allocation changes: highest current rate first, or proportional across remaining balances. A projection stops before any cycle whose assumed minimum exceeds the payment budget, or after 120 cycles. Unfinished interest totals are partial; no payoff saving is reported.

On this page

  1. Keep transaction balances and their rates separate
  2. Use the same explicit minimum assumption in both paths
  3. Follow the first payment into each bucket
  4. Compare complete repayment costs only when both schedules finish
  5. Keep a blocked or unfinished path visibly incomplete
  6. Read the rate-and-payment matrix beside the actual agreement
  7. Sources and scope
  8. Continue reading

The central idea

The same total payment can reduce different parts of a card balance. Interest cost depends on which balances remain, so the allocation rule belongs beside the payment amount and the rates.

01

Keep transaction balances and their rates separate

A credit card can contain amounts charged at different interest rates. A single total balance then hides information needed to understand the next interest charge and how a payment changes the account.

The FCAC explains that different transaction types can carry different rates and describes highest-rate-first or proportional treatment of amounts paid above the minimum. It also directs borrowers to the agreement for the issuer’s allocation rules. This calculator does not identify an actual card’s rules or calculate its legal minimum.

The example starts with CAD 5,000 in bucket A at an assumed 18% nominal annual rate and CAD 2,000 in bucket B at 30%. There are no new transactions, promotional expiries, fees, grace periods or rate changes. Interest is simplified to the opening monthly balance multiplied by its annual rate divided by twelve.

02

Use the same explicit minimum assumption in both paths

The illustrative minimum is the smaller of the interest-inclusive statement total and the greater of CAD 25 or the selected percentage of that total. The default percentage is 3%. It is a model parameter, not a statement about the minimum that applies to a particular borrower or province.

First-cycle interest is CAD 75 in bucket A and CAD 50 in bucket B. The total statement becomes CAD 7,125. Three percent gives an illustrative minimum of CAD 213.75. The selected fixed payment budget is CAD 300, leaving CAD 86.25 above that minimum.

For this comparison, the minimum portion is allocated proportionally to the two statement balances in both paths. That is an explicit shared assumption. It must not be read as the issuer’s actual treatment of the minimum. Keeping it identical isolates what changes when the excess CAD 86.25 is allocated by a different rule.

03

Follow the first payment into each bucket

The proportional minimum allocation sends CAD 152.25 to bucket A and CAD 61.50 to bucket B. Under highest-rate-first excess allocation, the remaining CAD 86.25 goes to bucket B because its entered rate is higher.

After that first payment, bucket A is CAD 4,922.75 and bucket B is CAD 1,902.25. Their total is CAD 6,825. Under proportional excess allocation, the whole CAD 300 payment follows the statement-balance weights. Bucket A ends at about CAD 4,861.32 and bucket B at about CAD 1,963.68.

Both totals are CAD 6,825 because the same CAD 125 interest was added and the same CAD 300 was paid. The difference appears in the mix remaining for the next cycle. The higher-rate balance is smaller under the first rule, so its next interest charge is smaller, even though the combined first-cycle debt is identical.

04

Compare complete repayment costs only when both schedules finish

Under the defaults, highest-rate-first excess allocation repays the combined debt in thirty cycles. Total interest is about CAD 1,929.91. Proportional excess allocation takes thirty-one cycles and incurs about CAD 2,169.54. The modeled full-payoff interest difference is about CAD 239.64.

The component bars show why each bucket need not have lower interest separately. Highest-first incurs about CAD 1,494.11 in bucket A and CAD 435.79 in bucket B. Proportional allocation incurs about CAD 1,248.02 and CAD 921.52 respectively. The increase in A’s interest is smaller than the reduction in B’s interest.

The result keeps the same total payment budget while debt remains, with the last payment capped at what is owed. It does not invest money released by an earlier payoff or compare the household’s wealth after later saving. Those would be additional cash flows with their own assumptions.

05

Keep a blocked or unfinished path visibly incomplete

If the entered payment is below the illustrative minimum for a cycle, the model stops before projecting that cycle. A CAD 100 payment cannot start the default schedule because it is below CAD 213.75. The tool does not invent an approved reduced payment or simulate an actual late-payment regime.

A one-point debt line therefore means no payment cycle could be projected under those assumptions. Interest and payments shown for an unfinished path cover completed modeled cycles only. They exclude the unprojected future and must not be called a lifetime cost.

The schedule also stops after 120 cycles if debt remains. A low payment can leave an unpaid balance or fail to offset interest under some entered terms. The payoff metric then reports no completed payoff, and the comparison with a full repayment cost is unavailable. No default fee, penalty rate or credit-reporting outcome is calculated.

06

Read the rate-and-payment matrix beside the actual agreement

The matrix changes bucket B’s rate and the fixed monthly payment budget. It reports an interest saving only when both hypothetical paths fully repay within the limit and meet their assumed minimums. Unavailable cells preserve that condition rather than treating an incomplete result as zero cost.

Bucket B is not always the higher-rate balance after edits. The highest-first method sorts the two actual entered rates. At equal rates, the allocation mix does not change the combined interest result under this simplified ledger. The chart labels retain A and B so that a rate edit does not silently change which balance is being followed.

For a real card, confirm each transaction balance, rate, minimum formula, payment allocation and processing date. Actual daily interest, grace periods and fees can materially change the statement. The graphs teach how an allocation rule changes a defined repayment ledger; they do not replace the agreement or supply instructions for a live payment.
